say: You give it an object and its image after an enlargement. It finds the **centre** of enlargement and the scale factor $k$.
The key idea: a line through a point and its image passes through the centre. Draw two such lines and they meet at the centre. Then $k$ is image length over object length.

how.higher: Higher level uses it as a part inside a longer Paper 2 geometry question, where $k$ is found from two matching lengths and then used for an area (5 marks of a 30-mark question).
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for it on Paper 2 as a construction of the centre, then measuring to find $k$, as part of a bigger question worth about 15 marks.

example.question:
The triangle $PQR$ is the image of the triangle $ABC$ under an enlargement.
(a) Construct the centre of enlargement and label it $O$.
(b) Given $|AB| = 4$ cm and $|PQ| = 10$ cm, find the scale factor $k$.
(c) Check your answer: $|OA| = 6$ cm. Find $|OP|$.

steps.title: Find the centre
steps.say: Join each point to its image. The lines meet at one point. That point is the **centre** $O$.

lines.text: Join $C$ to $R$ as a check. All three lines meet at $O$.

steps.title: Compare matching sides
steps.say: The scale factor is image length over object length. $|PQ|$ is the image of $|AB|$.

steps.title: Check with distances from O
steps.say: Distances from $O$ scale by the same $\hl{1}{k}$. Multiply $|OA|$ by $\hl{1}{k}$ to get $|OP|$.

lines.text: On the diagram you can measure $|OP|$ to confirm. Allow 5 mm either way.

higher.tip: Write the answer without worrying about the unit. The scheme accepts a correct answer with no unit, so spend the time on the working instead.
Show the length you use first. Finding one relevant length earns a step of its own, so write it down before you combine anything.

ordinary.tip: Draw the construction rays even if you cannot finish. Any attempt at a ray earns marks, and a second ray earns more.

sources.quote: An attempt to draw any construction ray

ordinary.tip: Measure carefully, but you have some room: the scheme allows a small tolerance on your measurements.
If you make a slip early, keep going. Later parts are marked from your own earlier work.

say: You give it two circles that touch at one point $T$. It tells you the two centres and $T$ lie on one straight line.
The key idea: both radii to $T$ are perpendicular to the same tangent. Two lines perpendicular to one line at one point are the same line.

example.question: Two circles touch externally at $T$. Their centres are $A$ and $B$. The radius of one circle is $4$ cm and the radius of the other is $9$ cm. Find $|AB|$.

steps.title: Draw the common tangent
steps.say: Draw the tangent to both circles at $T$. A radius meets a tangent at a right angle.

lines.text: $[AT]$ and $[BT]$ are both perpendicular to this tangent at $T$.

steps.title: Use Corollary 6
steps.say: Both radii are perpendicular to the same line at the same point. So $A$, $T$ and $B$ lie on one straight line. This is **Corollary 6**.

lines.text: For external touching, $T$ is between $A$ and $B$.

steps.title: Add the radii
steps.say: Along the line, $\hl{1}{|AB|}$ is made of the two radii.

lines.text: If the circles touched internally you would subtract: $9 - 4 = 5$.

say: You give it a quadrilateral with all four corners on a circle, a **cyclic quadrilateral**. It tells you each pair of opposite angles adds to $180°$.
The key idea: opposite angles stand on arcs that together make the whole circle. Write that sum as an equation and solve it.

example.question: $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral. $|\angle A| = (2x + 10)°$ and $|\angle C| = (3x - 20)°$. Find $x$.

steps.title: Spot opposite angles
steps.say: $A$ and $C$ are opposite corners of a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle.

lines.text: So Corollary 5 applies: opposite angles sum to $180°$.

steps.title: Write the equation
steps.say: Add the two angles and set the total equal to $180$.

steps.title: Solve for x
steps.say: Add $10$ to both sides, then divide by $5$ to find $\hl{1}{x}$.

lines.text: Check: $|\angle A| = 86°$ and $|\angle C| = 94°$. They add to $180°$.

say: You give it two angles at the circle that stand on the same **arc**. It tells you they are equal.
The key idea: each one is half the angle the arc makes at the centre. Same arc, same centre angle, so the two angles match.

how.higher: Higher level uses it as one step in a longer Paper 2 circle question, found by chasing angles in a diagram, worth part of 10 marks.

example.question: $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ are on a circle. $|\angle ACB| = (3x + 5)°$ and $|\angle ADB| = (5x - 25)°$. Find $x$.

steps.title: Find the shared arc
steps.say: Both angles are at the circle and both stand on the arc $AB$.

lines.text: $\angle ACB$ and $\angle ADB$ stand on the same arc.

steps.title: Apply Corollary 2
steps.say: Angles on the same arc are equal. This is **Corollary 2**. Set the two expressions equal.

steps.title: Solve for x
steps.say: Collect the $x$ terms on one side and the numbers on the other. Then divide to find $\hl{1}{x}$.

higher.tip: Give a reason with every angle you find. In Higher Paper 2 the reason in brackets, such as "standing on the same arc", is part of the marked solution.
Spot the angles that stand on the same arc. Showing two equal angles on one arc earns partial credit even if you go no further.
